785.title: Here am I; send me (Isaiah 6:1–8)
785.hook: seraphim, a live coal on the lips, and a prophet who volunteers
785.howItsDone: Jews say the seraphim's words, 'holy, holy, holy', in the Kedushah during the repetition of the Amidah, and it is a custom to rise on the toes at each 'holy'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a forge, and your line: war is learned, and unlearned. Did you reshape one sharp word? Today, we go back to the scene many readers take as Isaiah's call. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

"In the year that king Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and His train filled the temple." That's how Isaiah dates the vision: by a death. A king is gone, and in the Temple a man sees something that fills the whole space. Above the throne stand seraphim, burning ones, each with six wings: two to cover the face, two to cover the feet, two to fly. And they are calling to one another.
screen: `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.` → `HIGH AND LIFTED UP.` → `SERAPHIM CALLING.`

segments.voice: What they call is this: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; The whole earth is full of His glory." If you've been in a synagogue, you may have heard it. It's at the heart of the Kedushah, said during the leader's repetition of the Amidah, when people rise up on their toes at each holy. The doorposts shake. Smoke fills the house. And Isaiah's first words aren't brave at all: "Woe is me! for I am undone; Because I am a man of unclean lips, And I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips". He feels too small and too stained for the room. Then one of the seraphim takes a live coal from the altar with tongs, flies to him, and touches his mouth with it. "Lo, this hath touched thy lips; And thine iniquity is taken away". The lips he was ashamed of are the lips that get cleansed. Notice: the coal goes to the mouth, the very place a prophet will work. Then Isaiah hears a voice. Not addressed to him. A question into the room: "Whom shall I send, And who will go for us?" And he answers: "Here am I; send me." In Hebrew, the first word is hineni. Abraham says hineni when God calls him by name. So does Moses at the burning bush. But they were called by name. Isaiah wasn't. He heard an open question and stepped forward. And he said yes before he heard the job. The task that follows is a hard one, as the very next verses show. Hineni is not a promise that it'll be easy. It's a person saying: I'm here, I'm listening, use me.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME, A MAN OF UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A LIVE COAL TOUCHES HIS LIPS.` · then, large: `HERE AM I; SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: volunteer for one thing. Sit still for a breath or two. Then listen for the open questions around you, the ones nobody's answering. Who can drive? Who'll bring food? Who'll sit with her? Who'll take this on at work? If a voice in you says, like Isaiah, I'm not good enough for this, breathe through it. Then pick one open question you could answer this week. Quietly, try the word: hineni, here I am. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Hineni. "Here I am": Isaiah's answer to an open question in the Temple, given before he knew the task. Today's word.
Your line: here am I, send me. Today, when someone asks who can help, be the one who answers first. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 785 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOLF AND THE LAMB.`

786.title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9)
786.hook: the wolf dwells with the lamb, "and a little child shall lead them"
786.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 11 as a vision of the messianic age; it is read as the haftarah on the last day of Passover outside Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a live coal on the lips, and Isaiah's answer, hineni, here am I, send me. Did you answer one open question? Today the prophet paints a world worth volunteering for. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

Quick question: what lies down with the lamb? A familiar picture is the lion and the lamb, on greeting cards and paintings. But open Isaiah 11 and the lion isn't the one beside the lamb. The verse is stranger, and more crowded, than the greeting card. It starts with a tree. "And there shall come forth a shoot out of the stock of Jesse, And a twig shall grow forth out of his roots." From the family of Jesse, King David's father, a new shoot.
screen: `WHO LIES DOWN WITH THE LAMB?` → `NOT ON THE GREETING CARD.` → `A SHOOT FROM THE STOCK OF JESSE.`

segments.voice: Isaiah describes a coming king from David's line, filled with a spirit of wisdom and understanding, who judges the poor with righteousness. Then the picture widens from the palace to the whole of creation. "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, And the leopard shall lie down with the kid; And the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; And a little child shall lead them." So the wolf is with the lamb. The leopard lies down with the young goat. The lion is there too, and the next verse says it shall eat straw like the ox. Hunter after hunter is set beside its prey. And who's in charge of this strange herd? Not a king, not a soldier. A small child. A nursing baby plays by the hole of a snake. Then the reason: "They shall not hurt nor destroy In all My holy mountain; For the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, As the waters cover the sea." Jewish tradition reads this chapter as a picture of the messianic age. But how literally? Maimonides, the medieval teacher, wrote that the world will keep its natural order, and that the wolf and the lamb are a parable: Israel will dwell in safety among nations that once threatened it like wolves and leopards. Other readers take the animals more literally. Either way, the hope is the same. The ones who were dangerous to each other become neighbors, and the one leading them is a small, trusting child. Strength doesn't make the peace here. Knowledge of God, filling the earth like water fills the sea.
screen: `A KING WHO JUDGES THE POOR.` · `HUNTERS BESIDE THEIR PREY.` · then, large: `A LITTLE CHILD SHALL LEAD THEM.` · then: `AS THE WATERS COVER THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace between an unlikely pair. Let your breath find its own pace. Think of two people who don't get along, or two parts of your own life that keep clashing: two relatives, two coworkers, your work and your rest. Picture them side by side, like the wolf and the lamb, without anyone getting hurt. What would help them dwell together? Maybe something small and childlike: a shared meal, a joke, an honest question. Choose one simple step you could take. If you pray, you can ask for peace between them. The bell holds the time.
Holy mountain. The mountain in Isaiah's vision where the wolf lies with the lamb and nothing hurts or destroys, led by a little child. Today's word.
Your line: a little child leads. Today, try the simplest, most childlike way into a tense moment: a plain question, a kind word, an invitation to sit together. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

787.title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40:1–2)
787.hook: after Tisha B'Av, prophetic readings of comfort begin
787.howItsDone: Isaiah 40 is read in synagogue on Shabbat Nachamu, the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, and Jews visiting a house of mourning traditionally offer a set line of comfort that names the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the holy mountain, the wolf and the lamb lay down together, and a little child leads them. Did an unlikely pair make peace anywhere near you? Today, Isaiah turns a page and changes his voice. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

Chapter thirty-nine of Isaiah holds a warning: the treasures of the king's house will one day be carried off to Babylon. Then chapter forty opens with a different sound entirely. Not a warning. Not a reason. Two words, the same word twice: Nachamu, nachamu. Comfort, comfort. There is a Shabbat in the Jewish year named after that word. It comes right after Tisha B'Av, the fast of mourning for the fallen Temple, and synagogues read these verses on it. A day of grief, and then, the very next Shabbat, comfort.
screen: `A WARNING ABOUT BABYLON.` → `THEN: NACHAMU, NACHAMU.` → `THE SHABBAT AFTER TISHA B'AV.`

segments.voice: Here is how the chapter begins, in the King James words: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." Notice the ye. The command is plural. God isn't comforting the people directly here; God is telling a group, unnamed, to go and do it. Some readers hear prophets, some hear angels, some hear anyone within earshot. Comfort, in this verse, is a job handed out. And the word is doubled. Comfort, comfort. Once wasn't enough. Then the next line: "Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem." The Hebrew is warmer than the English. It says, literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem. Not at her. Not about her. To her heart. And what are the comforters told to say? That her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received double for all her sins. This comfort doesn't pretend nothing happened. It names the war. It names the wrong. It just says: it is over now. That shape lives on in an ordinary Jewish custom. When people visit a house of mourning, there is a traditional sentence said to the mourners as they leave, asking that God comfort them among the other mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. Same word for comfort. Same city. The private loss in one living room is set beside the old loss of a whole people, and both are spoken to the heart. Comfort, in this chapter, is less a feeling than a visit.
screen: `THE COMMAND IS PLURAL.` · `COMFORT, COMFORT: SAID TWICE.` · `SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.` · `IT NAMES THE LOSS, THEN SAYS: IT IS OVER.` · then, large: `COMFORT YE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort one person. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who is carrying something heavy right now: a loss, a diagnosis, a long hard season. Don't solve it. Just ask what speaking to their heart would sound like. Not advice. Not a reason. Maybe just: I'm thinking of you. I'm here. Decide how you'll say it today, a call, a note, a visit. If you pray, you can hold the verse's two words for them: comfort, comfort. The bell holds the time.
Nachamu. Comfort ye, a plural command, said twice at the start of Isaiah forty, and the name of the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av. Today's word.
Your line: comfort ye my people. Today, send the message you decided on, and speak to the heart, not at it. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

788.title: Wings as eagles (Isaiah 40:31)
788.hook: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength"
788.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 40 as part of the prophetic readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av, and Shabbat is the weekly practice of stopping work so that body and spirit can rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachamu: comfort, comfort, a job handed out to a group. Your line was comfort ye my people. Did your message reach someone's heart? Today, the end of the same chapter. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

Near the end of Isaiah forty, the prophet quotes the people's complaint back to them. Jacob is saying: my way is hidden from the Lord, my cause is passed over. Nobody sees what this is costing me. The prophet answers with a question, hast thou not known?, and says the Lord fainteth not. Then he grants that the tiredness is real for people, and goes further: even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall. The strongest runners in town give out. So where does strength come from, if not from being young? The chapter's last verse answers, and it's a verse with wings in it.
screen: `MY WAY IS HIDDEN FROM THE LORD.` → `EVEN THE YOUNG FALL.` → `THE LAST VERSE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The verse reads: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Start with the condition. Not they that try harder. Not they that are young. They that wait. In this verse, strength isn't something you grind out; it's something given back while you wait. Some translations render that verb as they that hope. Now look at the order of the promise. Fly. Run. Walk. If you were writing a pep talk, you'd build up: walk, then run, then soar. Isaiah goes the other way. Some readers hear that as honest. There are days of wings. There are days you can run. And there are plenty of days when the most anyone can promise is that you'll walk and not faint. The verse counts that as strength too, and lists it last, where it has the final word. And the eagle itself: the Hebrew word is nesher, a great bird of the open sky. Some readers picture it rising on what's already moving in the air, not flapping its way up. Waiting, in this verse, looks less like doing nothing and more like that: being still enough to be carried. Jewish life builds that stillness into the week. Shabbat is one way a whole people practices stopping, so the strength can come back.
screen: `THEY THAT WAIT, OR THEY THAT HOPE.` · `FLY, RUN, WALK: THE ORDER GOES DOWN.` · `WALK, AND NOT FAINT, IS STRENGTH TOO.` · `AN EAGLE RISES ON MOVING AIR.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in order to renew. Until the bell, don't fix anything, plan anything or check anything. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Let today be whatever kind of day it is: a wings day, a running day, or a walking day. All three count. Just wait. If you pray, you can hold the verse's first words: they that wait upon the Lord. The bell holds the time.
Nesher. Hebrew for eagle, the bird in Isaiah forty, thirty-one: those who wait shall renew their strength, mount up, run, and walk and not faint. Today's word.
Your line: renew your strength. Today, take one real pause before you're empty, not after. And if it's a walking day, walking and not fainting counts. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

screen: `DAY 788 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LIGHT OF THE NATIONS.`

789.title: A light of the nations (Isaiah 42:6)
789.hook: Israel is called to be "a light of the nations"
789.howItsDone: Isaiah 42 is read in synagogue as a haftarah, and the phrase a light to the nations is used in Jewish teaching for the calling of the people Israel, understood in different ways by different communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nesher, wings as eagles: fly, run, walk and not faint. Your line was renew your strength. Did you pause before you were empty? Today, a calling with a lamp in it. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Chapter forty-two introduces a figure the book calls my servant, and before this chapter says the word light, we learn what this servant won't do. "He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench". No shouting. No snapping what's already cracked. No blowing out a flame that's nearly gone. Then, a few lines later, comes the calling.
screen: `A BRUISED REED. A SMOKING WICK.` → `NO SHOUTING IN THE STREET.` → `THEN, THE CALLING.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in verse six: "I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand." And then: I will give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the nations. The King James says Gentiles; the Hebrew word, goyim, means nations, and that's how the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it. So who is the servant? Jewish tradition hears the people Israel in these chapters, and we'll come back to the servant in a few days. Today, stay with the light. Look at what kind of light it is. It doesn't shout. It doesn't break the bruised reed. It doesn't snuff out the smoking wick. This is not a searchlight sweeping the streets. It's closer to a lamp in a window: it's simply there, and people find their way by it. And the next verse says what the light is for: "To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison." Light, in Isaiah, is something that frees people. Jewish writers have taken this calling in different ways. Some hear it as a call to live by the Torah so faithfully that others notice. Some hear it as a call to justice, opening eyes and prison doors. Some hear it mainly as a promise held by God: I will hold thine hand. What they share is that the light is a calling, not a trophy. A lamp doesn't light itself to be admired. It lights the room.
screen: `NO SHOUTING, NO BREAKING THE REED.` · `I WILL HOLD THINE HAND.` · `GOYIM: THE NATIONS.` · `TO OPEN THE BLIND EYES.` · then, large: `A LIGHT OF THE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a light for one person. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who is a bit of a bruised reed right now, cracked but not broken, or a wick that's burning low. Don't plan anything loud. Ask the quiet question: what small thing would help them see their way today? A word of credit. A door held open. An answer to the message they sent. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold the verse: I will hold thine hand. The bell holds the time.
A light of the nations. From Isaiah forty-two: a servant called to be a covenant of the people and a light that opens eyes. Today's word.
screen: `A LIGHT OF THE NATIONS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a light to the nations. Today, do the quiet thing you chose, for the one person, and don't break anything that's already bruised. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

790.title: Through the waters (Isaiah 43:2)
790.hook: "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee"
790.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 43 among the prophets' words of comfort to the exiles, and its promise of God's presence in hard times is a verse some turn to in illness, grief and danger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a light of the nations: a quiet lamp that won't break a bruised reed. Your line was a light to the nations. Who did you light the way for? Day seven hundred ninety.

"Fear not." Two words, early in Isaiah forty-three, and then a run of reasons, said to a people far from home: "I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Not a crowd. A name. And the very next verse turns to water and fire, and in the King James it doesn't say if. It says when. When the water is up to your chest. When the river is moving faster than you are. When the fire is close enough to feel. That small word, when, is where today begins.
screen: `FEAR NOT.` → `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.` → `NOT IF. WHEN.`

segments.voice: Then verse two: "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned." Read it slowly, and notice what it doesn't promise. It doesn't promise there will be no waters. It doesn't promise a bridge, or a detour, or a dry season. It promises company: I will be with thee. And it promises a limit: the rivers shall not overflow thee. The water comes up. It doesn't close over your head. And look at the verbs. Passest through. Walkest through. The person in this verse keeps moving. Nobody is told to stand still in the river, or to camp in the fire. Through means there is another side. Some readers hear the people's own story in the water and the river. A sea split open when they left Egypt. A river held back when they crossed into the land. Isaiah's listeners, far from home, are reminded that they have walked through water before. The verse doesn't explain why the hard thing comes. It doesn't say the fire is a lesson. It simply stands in the water beside them. In the chapter, that's the whole of the comfort: you are named, you are not alone in it, and it will not cover you.
screen: `NO PROMISE OF A DRY ROAD.` · `A PROMISE OF COMPANY, AND A LIMIT.` · `THROUGH MEANS ANOTHER SIDE.` · `THEY HAD WALKED THROUGH WATER BEFORE.` · then, large: `I WILL BE WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold on through one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Name the water you're in right now, the thing that feels deeper than you'd like. Don't try to drain it. Just notice where it reaches. Your ankles? Your chest? Notice whether your head is still above it. Breathe there. Then take one small step through it today, not around it: one call, one form, one honest conversation. If you pray, you can hold the verse: I will be with thee. The bell holds the time.
Isaiah, who promised a people far from home that passing through deep water or fire would come with company, and with a limit: it would not close over them.
Your line: the waters won't overflow. Today, take your one step through, and when it feels deep, check: your head is still above it. Day seven hundred ninety.

791.title: I will not forget thee (Isaiah 49:15)
791.hook: even if a mother could forget her child, God will not
791.howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 49 among the prophetic readings of comfort in the weeks after Tisha B'Av, and visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is counted in Jewish life as a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah's promise: not if, but when, and company in the river. Your line was the waters won't overflow. Did you take your step through? Day seven hundred ninety-one.

"But Zion said, The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me." Isaiah gives the city a voice, and that's what she says. Not a polite question. A charge. You left. You forgot. It's the voice of someone who has waited by the phone for so long that waiting has turned into certainty. The chapter doesn't scold her for saying it. It doesn't tell her she's wrong to feel it. It answers her, and the answer reaches for the closest bond anyone knows.
screen: `ZION SAYS: I'VE BEEN FORGOTTEN.` → `A CHARGE, NOT A QUESTION.` → `THE CHAPTER ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The answer comes as a question: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Look at the image God chooses. Not a king remembering a subject. Not a master remembering a servant. A nursing mother and her baby. In this verse, God's memory is compared to a mother's. And then the surprising honesty: yea, they may forget. The verse admits that even the strongest human bond can fail. Mothers can be overwhelmed, or ill, or gone. The prophet doesn't pretend otherwise. The prophet reaches for the strongest bond he knows, and then has God say that even if that bond fails, this one holds. And the next verse gives a picture you can almost hold: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands." Graven, engraved, cut in. Not a note on a scrap of paper that can be lost. Written into the hand itself, the way someone writes a thing on their palm so they'll see it every time they reach for anything. Thy walls are continually before me. Zion's broken walls, always in view. For people who felt erased by exile, this is the reply: you are not a name on a list somewhere. You are in the palm. Jewish tradition reads these chapters in the weeks of comfort after mourning. The complaint is allowed. And the answer is: I will not forget thee.
screen: `A NURSING MOTHER AND HER CHILD.` · `YEA, THEY MAY FORGET.` · `GRAVEN ON THE PALMS OF MY HANDS.` · `THY WALLS ARE CONTINUALLY BEFORE ME.` · then, large: `YET WILL I NOT FORGET THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone forgotten. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind go to someone who has dropped out of view. An old neighbor. A relative in a care home. A friend who stopped showing up and nobody asked why. A colleague who left. Let their face come back. Say their name to yourself. Then decide on one way to let them know they weren't forgotten: a call, a card, a visit. If you pray, you can hold the verse: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands. The bell holds the time.
Zion, the city given a voice to say she'd been forgotten, and answered: even if a mother could forget her child, I will not forget thee.
